newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH PM SAYS AMSTERDAM STRENGTHENED EMU PLAN.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH PM SAYS AMSTERDAM STRENGTHENED EMU PLAN.

text.p: Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said on Wednesday that the European Union summit earlier this week in Amsterdam had strengthened the process towards economic and monetary union (EMU).

Lipponen, speaking at a news conference after briefing parliament's grand committee on the outcome of the summit, repeated Finland's view that convergence criteria for membership of the single currency should be strictly adhered to.
"There was a certain kind of crisis but its outcome strengthened the EMU plan," Lipponen said, referring to EU leaders' struggle to reach agreement on the budget stability pact.
He said EU leaders would review towards the end of 1997 which countries could be eligible to join the single currency area in the first wave from 1999.

"There will be an overall assessment ... we will maintain that the criteria must be strictly adhered to, and we cannot think that we would start selecting member countries politically," Lipponen said.
He said the new euro currency could be on the softer side if EMU took off with very many of the EU's 15 member countries on board.
"If EMU were very broad, then the euro could be somewhat weaker," Lipponen said.
But he said Finland and other EU members were aiming for a credible euro.
"We are targetting a credible euro and I don't doubt that the other member countries are aiming for that too," he said.
A narrow EMU on the other hand would "create uncertainty in outside countries, and through that for the whole European economy," he added.
Lipponen said the assessments on EMU participants would involve looking at the overall economic benefits for Europe.
"We must make an overall assessment on what is the most wise for Finland and for European economic stability," he said.
Lipponen said too little attention had been paid to the fact that "eventually all countries, including France, wanted to confirm the stability pact".
